The US also wants to boost its military spending over the next 12 months by more than £100bn. "We believe that it is in the national interest to increase Nato's annual military budget by about 60% over the next 15 years," US defence secretary Chuck Hagel said in a statement on Monday. The Pentagon currently spends about $1.7bn on security and defence programs, including the £1bn in training that the military needs to help Ukraine and other countries to combat Russian aggression.

The deal has been hailed by NATO's defence ministers as a "historic breakthrough" in Kiev's efforts to fight back the crisis in eastern Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels on Monday, US Secretary of State John Kerry said that the agreement was a "game-changing step in the fight against the Ukrainian armed forces". He said that Russia's "military modernization programme must be accelerated, and that we must continue to provide a clear and effective deterrent to this aggression". Nato's chief executive, Anders Fogh Rasmussen, said that the deal was "a huge step forward for Europe". "This is a strategic victory for the two countries," he said. "We are confident that the Russian army will continue to grow, and will be able to meet its own needs in the coming months, while Russia is prepared to develop a defensive posture." NATO's top commander in Europe, General Anders Fogh Rasmussen, said: "This agreement is a historic breakthrough. It demonstrates the strength of NATO's commitment to the fight against terror and extremism, and the ability to cope with the challenges posed by the new challenges created in the recent years. "We are pleased that we can now sign the first round of this agreement in Brussels. "The agreement now gives us a new basis for assessing the security of our allies and partners in Europe, and we will continue to work with our partners to ensure a sustainable, secure and credible security environment for all the alliance members," he said in a statement.
